<p>When your doctor tells you during pregnancy, "You have gestational diabetes," your first reaction might be fear or guilt. Questions like "Did I eat too much candy?" or "Will something happen to my baby?" might spin in your head.</p><p>Stay calm. Gestational diabetes (or <strong>pregnancy sugar</strong> as it's commonly known) is a very common condition occurring in about 10% of pregnant women. This diagnosis doesn't mean you're a "bad mother" or necessarily a sweets addict. It is simply your body's reaction to pregnancy hormones.</p><p>The good news is that with proper control and nutrition, you can have a completely healthy pregnancy and give birth to a healthy baby. Let's explore the solutions to this "sweet" problem together.</p><h2>What is gestational diabetes and why does it occur?</h2><p>Normally, when we eat, blood sugar levels rise and the pancreas secretes <strong>insulin</strong>. Insulin acts as a "key" that allows sugar to enter cells and be converted into energy.</p><p>During pregnancy, the placenta produces various hormones for the baby's development. However, these hormones sometimes interfere with the work of insulin (this is called <strong>insulin resistance</strong>). The mother's pancreas must produce more insulin to compensate for this situation. If the body cannot produce enough insulin, blood sugar levels rise and gestational diabetes occurs.</p><h2>Symptoms: How does it manifest?</h2><p>The most insidious part of gestational diabetes is that it often <strong>shows no symptoms</strong>. A woman may feel completely normal. However, when sugar levels are very high, the following symptoms may be observed:</p><ul><li><p><strong>Unbearable thirst:</strong> A constant desire to drink water.</p></li><li><p><strong>Frequent urination:</strong> While this is normal in pregnancy, it becomes more intense during diabetes.</p></li><li><p><strong>Dry mouth.</strong></p></li><li><p><strong>Fatigue.</strong></p></li></ul><p></p><p>Because it often goes unnoticed, a <strong>"Glucose Tolerance Test" (OGTT)</strong> is recommended for all pregnant women between <strong>24-28 weeks</strong> of pregnancy. This test is the only accurate way to make a diagnosis.</p><h2>What are the risks for the baby?</h2><p>If sugar is not kept under control, it can pose some risks for both mother and baby:</p><ul><li><p><strong>Large fetus (Macrosomia):</strong> Excess sugar in the mother's blood passes to the baby. The baby's body produces a lot of insulin in response, which causes rapid weight gain (especially in the shoulder and abdominal area). Babies heavier than 4 kg can have a difficult birth.</p></li><li><p><strong>Premature birth:</strong> High sugar can cause an increase in amniotic fluid (polyhydramnios) and early contractions.</p></li><li><p><strong>Postpartum hypoglycemia:</strong> Immediately after birth, the baby's blood sugar can drop suddenly (because they were used to high sugar in the womb).</p></li><li><p><strong>Future risk:</strong> These children have a slightly higher risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes in the future.</p></li></ul><blockquote><p>Remember: These risks only arise when sugar remains uncontrolled. Babies of mothers who follow their diet are usually born completely healthy.</p></blockquote><p>></p><h2>The basis of treatment: Nutrition and Diet</h2><p>80-90% of women with gestational diabetes can maintain normal sugar levels through proper nutrition alone, without the need for medication. Here are the main rules:</p><h3>1. Choose carbohydrates wisely</h3><p>Sugar cannot be cut out completely because the baby needs energy for development. However, you must replace <strong>"bad"</strong> carbohydrates with <strong>"good"</strong> ones.</p><ul><li><p>⛔ <strong>Stay away (Simple carbohydrates):</strong> White bread, white rice (pilaf), sugar, cakes, cookies, sugary sodas, fruit juices. These spike sugar suddenly.</p></li><li><p>✅ <strong>Accept (Complex carbohydrates):</strong> Whole wheat bread, buckwheat, bulgur, oats, legumes (lentils, chickpeas). These are absorbed slowly into the blood.</p></li></ul><p></p><h3>2. Eat frequently and in small portions</h3><p>Instead of 3 large meals a day, have <strong>3 main meals and 2-3 snacks</strong> (interim meals). This prevents sharp fluctuations in blood sugar.</p><h3>3. Protein and Vegetables are your friends</h3><p>Every meal should include protein (meat, fish, eggs, cottage cheese) and plenty of vegetables (cucumber, tomato, greens, cabbage). Fibrous vegetables slow down the absorption of sugar into the blood.</p><h3>4. Pay attention to fruits</h3><p>Fruits are beneficial but contain sugar.</p><ul><li><p>Stay away from grapes, figs, melons, and watermelons (they have too much sugar).</p></li><li><p>Prefer apples, pears, oranges, and berries (strawberries, raspberries).</p></li><li><p>Don't eat fruit alone; eat it with a handful of walnuts or a slice of cheese (protein reduces the effect of sugar).</p></li></ul><p></p><h2>How to measure sugar? (Glucometer)</h2><p>Your doctor will ask you to measure your sugar at home. For this, you should buy a small device – a <strong>glucometer</strong>.</p><ul><li><p><strong>Morning fasting:</strong> The norm should usually be below 95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/l).</p></li><li><p><strong>1 hour after a meal:</strong> Below 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/l).</p></li><li><p><strong>2 hours after a meal:</strong> Below 120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/l).</p></li></ul><p></p><p><em>(Target numbers may vary according to your doctor).</em></p><h2>If the need for insulin arises...</h2><p>If sugar does not drop despite the diet, your doctor may prescribe <strong>insulin injections</strong> or pills. Do not be afraid of this at all.</p><ul><li><p>Insulin does not cross the placenta and does not harm the baby.</p></li><li><p>This does not mean you are "incapable"; your placenta is simply producing very strong hormones.</p></li><li><p>Insulin is temporary and will be stopped after birth.</p></li></ul><p></p><h2>What happens after birth?</h2><p>Good news: As soon as the baby is born, the placenta is expelled from the body and diabetes usually disappears immediately. However, your doctor will want to check you again 6-12 weeks after delivery.</p><p>Gestational diabetes is a warning bell, but not a sentence. It can be turned into an opportunity that forces you to eat healthier and monitor your weight throughout pregnancy. As a result, both you stay in shape and your baby develops healthily.</p><p>You can use the <strong>Anacan app</strong> to track your nutrition regimen, monitor weight gain, and record your sugar measurements. May you hold your baby in health!</p>
